records.sourceFile: Relationship between Pre-Training     Subjective Wellness Measures, Player Load and Rating of Perceived   Exertion   Training Load in American College Football.pdf

paper.citation: Govus AD, Coutts AJ, Duffield R, Murray A, Fullagar HHK. Relationship Between Pretraining Subjective Wellness Measures, Player Load, and Rating-of-Perceived-Exertion Training Load in American College Football. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018;13(1):95-101.
paper.abstract: A retrospective cohort study examined relationships between subjective wellness, GPS-derived player load, and session-RPE load in collegiate American football.
paper.tldr: Wellness and energy had only trivial associations with player load, while soreness related trivially to session-RPE load. Use subjective reports as one input to individual monitoring, not a readiness verdict.
paper.methods: Fifty-eight Division I American football players were monitored during three weekly sessions over eight late-season weeks. Five-point wellness ratings, GPS and accelerometry player load, and session RPE were analyzed with linear mixed models.
paper.findings: A one-unit increase in wellness Z score and energy corresponded to 2.3% and 2.6% higher player load, respectively; lower soreness was trivially associated with lower session-RPE load.
paper.limitations: The analysis was retrospective and from one team, used a custom unvalidated wellness questionnaire, omitted indoor GPS sessions, and covered only mid- to late-season observations.
paper.practicalImplications: Collect simple wellness, external-load, and internal-load data together, look for within-athlete patterns, and use discussion and context before changing training.
paper.athleteDev: Encourage honest reporting of sleep, energy, and soreness and explain that one low score opens a conversation rather than determining participation.
paper.rtp: During reconditioning, interpret wellness with symptoms, objective progression, and the planned exposure. A questionnaire cannot independently clear return to practice.

records.sourceFile: Severe exercise associated              hyponatremia in a collegiate American footbal player.pdf

paper.citation: Changstrom B, Brill J, Hecht S. Severe Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia in a Collegiate American Football Player. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2017;16(5):343-345.
paper.abstract: This case report describes severe exercise-associated hyponatremia in a collegiate American football player after excessive hypotonic fluid consumption.
paper.tldr: Excess fluid can mimic or coexist with common exertional complaints. Headache, vomiting, and neurologic symptoms need prompt medical assessment rather than an automatic dehydration response.
paper.methods: A 21-year-old Division III football defensive back was clinically evaluated after competition, with laboratory testing, follow-up, and retrospective fluid-intake history reported.
paper.findings: After consuming about 5 L water the night before, 5 L hypotonic sports drink before the game, and more hypotonic fluid during play, the athlete developed symptoms with sodium 124 mmol/L; sodium normalized by follow-up.
paper.limitations: One case cannot estimate risk or establish a hydration prescription, and the climate, intake pattern, clinical assessment, and management may not transfer to other athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Use individualized, medically governed hydration plans and a symptom- and sodium-aware emergency pathway; avoid reflexively giving more hypotonic fluid for every exertional complaint.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to drink to an individualized plan and immediately report nausea, vomiting, headache, confusion, or worsening cramps.
paper.rtp: Return decisions after an exertional illness require medical confirmation of recovery and a reviewed hydration plan, not symptom resolution alone.

records.sourceFile: The effect of tissue flossing on ankle range of motion, jump, and sprint performance in elite rugby union athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Mills B, Mayo B, Tavares F, Driller M. The Effect of Tissue Flossing on Ankle Range of Motion, Jump, and Sprint Performance in Elite Rugby Union Athletes. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(3):282-286.
paper.abstract: A counterbalanced crossover experiment tested immediate ankle flossing effects on range of motion, jump, and sprint outcomes in professional rugby athletes.
paper.tldr: Two minutes of ankle flossing did not produce significant short-term performance or range-of-motion effects in this small elite-rugby sample.
paper.methods: Fourteen professional male rugby-union athletes completed floss and control trials one week apart. Lunge, countermovement-jump, and 20-m sprint tests were assessed before and 5 and 30 minutes after treatment.
paper.findings: There were no significant treatment-by-time interactions. Small effect-size differences favored flossing for countermovement performance at five minutes and selected sprint splits at 30 minutes.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and male, outcomes ended at 30 minutes, and the study did not test injury prevention, repeated use, or long-term training adaptation.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not prioritize tissue flossing for performance enhancement. If used as a preference-based warm-up adjunct, compare it against established preparation and athlete response.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid presenting transient modalities as performance shortcuts; reinforce progressive warm-up, movement quality, and task preparation.
paper.rtp: A flossing response is not a rehabilitation milestone. Progress ankle function through symptoms, strength, movement, and sport-specific exposure.

records.sourceFile: The influence of weekly sprint volume and maximal velocity exposures on eccentric hamstring strength in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Shah S, Collins K, Macgregor LJ. The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players. Sports. 2022;10(8):125.
paper.abstract: This cohort study related weekly GPS sprint exposure to weekly eccentric hamstring-strength change in professional male football players.
paper.tldr: Seven to eight weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were associated with small decreases in eccentric hamstring strength; this observational result is not a universal exposure limit.
paper.methods: Fifty-eight professional male footballers were observed over 1.5 seasons. Training and match GPS data and weekly eccentric hamstring-strength testing were analyzed for sprint-distance and velocity-exposure relationships.
paper.findings: Weekly sprint distance and efforts above 90% of maximum velocity had small inverse associations with strength change. Seven to eight efforts above 90% differed from lower categories; efforts above 95% were not associated.
paper.limitations: Causality cannot be inferred; the highest-speed exposures were limited, GPS has constraints at maximal velocity, and injury outcomes were not directly evaluated.
paper.practicalImplications: Track high-speed exposure and eccentric strength within each player's current preparation, total load, and response rather than applying a fixed weekly sprint count.
paper.athleteDev: Progress high-speed exposure gradually and report unusual hamstring symptoms or fatigue; a weekly count alone does not define safe readiness.
paper.rtp: Use staged sprint exposure with strength, symptoms, repeated-speed tolerance, and sport demands. Do not use this study's categories as return-to-play cutoffs.

records.sourceFile: The loading impact of training and match-play on non-contact muscle injuries in elite male soccer players - A seasonal analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Morgans R, Oliveira R, Mandorino M, Zmijewski P, Ryan B, Modric T, Teixeira J, Moreira A. The Loading Impact of Training and Match-Play on Non-Contact Muscle Injuries in Elite Male Soccer Players: A Seasonal Analysis. Biology of Sport. 2026;43:107-114.
paper.abstract: A single-club retrospective analysis modeled acute and chronic GPS load metrics preceding non-contact muscle injuries in elite male soccer.
paper.tldr: Higher recent high-speed and sprint distance were associated with lower modeled injury risk, while acute peak speed and chronic total distance were associated with higher risk. The small, synthetic-balanced model requires caution.
paper.methods: Thirty English Premier League outfield players were tracked for one season with GPS. Seven- and 28-day load variables were modeled against 12 non-contact muscle injuries using logistic regression after synthetic minority oversampling.
paper.findings: Higher acute high-speed-running and sprint-distance volume were protective in the model, whereas acute peak speed and chronic total distance were associated with increased risk.
paper.limitations: One season, one team, starting players, and 12 injuries limit power and generalizability. Oversampling can overfit, and internal load, gym work, recovery, and injury history were not included.
paper.practicalImplications: Review exposure trends alongside player history, current fitness, symptoms, and recovery. Validate any locally derived model before using it to influence loading.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes understand that load numbers guide discussion and planning; they do not predict an individual injury or replace reporting.
paper.rtp: Rebuild running exposure with clinical and performance criteria, then evaluate response to repeated high-speed and peak-speed demands in context.

records.sourceFile: Quantifying demands on the hamstrings during high-speed running - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: McNally T, Edwards S, Halaki M, O'Dwyer N, Pizzari T, Blyton S. Quantifying Demands on the Hamstrings During High-Speed Running: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2023;33(12):2423-2443.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized hamstring activation and kinetic demand during high-speed running.
paper.tldr: Hamstring activation and kinetic demands rise with running speed. Use this to inform progressive exposure, not to prescribe one universal sprint or force target.
paper.methods: Medline, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, SportDiscus, and Cochrane databases were searched under PRISMA 2020. Ninety-six studies of healthy adults running at specified speed thresholds were included.
paper.findings: Fast running produced pooled lateral-hamstring activation of 108.1% MVIC. Swing-phase peak knee-flexion internal moment and power rose with speed, with pooled moment of 2.2 Nm/kg during fast running.
paper.limitations: Studies varied in speed definitions, protocols, muscles, participants, and biomechanical methods. Laboratory measures in mostly healthy adults do not determine a prevention or rehabilitation dose.
paper.practicalImplications: Progress sprint exposure to representative speed and force demands while considering individual capacity, tissue tolerance, mechanics, and total workload.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that sprint preparation requires gradually earned exposure to high force and speed rather than avoidance of demanding movement.
paper.rtp: Use sprinting progression to restore high-speed demands, but combine it with symptoms, strength, capacity, and sport-specific decision criteria.

records.sourceFile: Reactive strength index and its associations with measures of physical and sports performance - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Jarvis P, Turner A, Read P, Bishop C. Reactive Strength Index and its Associations with Measures of Physical and Sports Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;52(2):301-330.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated associations between rebound-jump reactive strength index and physical or sporting performance.
paper.tldr: RSI relates moderately to several performance measures, but the relationship depends on the test and does not establish that increasing RSI will improve sport performance.
paper.methods: Thirty-two studies from PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, and Ovid met protocol and independent-performance-measure criteria. Random-effects meta-analysis assessed associations and heterogeneity.
paper.findings: RSI was moderately associated with strength and endurance and inversely associated with acceleration, top-speed time, and change-of-direction time. Small-study bias was apparent for acceleration and change-of-direction analyses.
paper.limitations: Protocols, drop heights, limbs, samples, sex, sport, and training status varied. The evidence is associational and may not transfer across testing methods.
paper.practicalImplications: Use one standardized rebound-jump protocol, interpret RSI alongside force, jump, speed, and exposure data, and track meaningful within-athlete change.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that RSI describes a test response, not a complete athletic identity or automatic target.
paper.rtp: Do not clear return from RSI alone. Pair standardized jump testing with symptoms, strength, movement, running exposure, and sport participation.

records.sourceFile: Reactive strength index as a key performance indicator in different athlete populations - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Southey B, Willshire M, Connick MJ, Austin D, Spits D, Beckman E. Reactive Strength Index as a Key Performance Indicator in Different Athlete Populations: A Systematic Review. Science & Sports. 2024;39(2):129-143.
paper.abstract: This systematic review assessed reactive-strength-index differences across athlete populations and associated physical characteristics.
paper.tldr: RSI often distinguishes athlete groups, with relative strength an important contributor. It remains a context-dependent test outcome rather than a stand-alone key performance indicator.
paper.methods: A systematic search screened 865 articles and included 19 studies. Results were narratively synthesized because study comparisons were not suitable for pooled analysis.
paper.findings: Moderate-to-large RSI differences predominated between athlete populations. Relative strength differentiated RSI performance, and included comparisons generally found higher RSI in faster athletes.
paper.limitations: No quantitative pooling was performed; tests and athlete groupings differed, and cohort comparisons cannot establish causal links between RSI and individual sport performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Use consistent local protocols and compare athletes against their own trend and relevant role context before pursuing strength or plyometric interventions.
paper.athleteDev: Frame RSI as feedback about a specific rebound task and reinforce that technical skill, strength, and exposure contribute to performance.
paper.rtp: Use RSI only as one standardized component of lower-limb capacity assessment, never as the sole return-to-sport criterion.

records.sourceFile: Resistance training load effects on muscle hypertrophy and strength gain - Systematic review and network meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Lopez P, Radaelli R, Taaffe DR, Newton RU, Galvão DA, Trajano GS, Teodoro J, Kraemer WJ, Häkkinen K, Pinto RS. Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020;53(6):1206-1216.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and network meta-analysis compared low-, moderate-, and high-load resistance training performed to volitional failure in healthy adults.
paper.tldr: When sets were taken to failure, different loads produced similar hypertrophy; higher loads ranked better for one-repetition-maximum strength. Program choices still need to fit the athlete and task.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided searches through December 2019 found 28 eligible healthy-adult experimental studies; 24 contributed hypertrophy and 23 strength data to network meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Low-, moderate-, and high-load training to failure had similar hypertrophy effects. Higher-load training ranked more favorably for 1-RM strength gain.
paper.limitations: Results apply to training to failure and 1-RM outcomes. Participants were mostly untrained or recreationally trained, and intervention, muscle-group, and test differences limit transfer.
paper.practicalImplications: Select loading according to strength specificity, hypertrophy goal, skill, tolerance, equipment, and time. Failure is not automatically required in a sport program.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes understand that a range of loads can build muscle, while heavier practice is more specific to maximal lifting strength.
paper.rtp: Match resistance loading to tissue tolerance and task demands, progressing volume and intensity without treating a meta-analysis ranking as a rehabilitation prescription.

records.sourceFile: Science or hype - Non-invasive brain stimulation and sport-specific performance - Evidence from a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Wang Q, Zhong J, Bao H, Wang Y. Science or Hype? Non-invasive Brain Stimulation and Sport-Specific Performance: Evidence from a Systematic Review and Three-Level Meta-analysis. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2026;44(6):700-723.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and three-level meta-analysis evaluated non-invasive brain stimulation for sport-specific performance.
paper.tldr: All included studies used tDCS and the pooled effect was small with low-quality evidence. It is not ready to support routine performance use.
paper.methods: Twenty-five eligible studies yielded 64 independent effect sizes. Three-level meta-analysis estimated overall effect and moderators for sport skill and stimulation target.
paper.findings: The pooled effect was small but significant (Hedges g=0.35) with considerable heterogeneity. Larger estimates appeared in open-skill sports and motor executive targets; evidence quality was low.
paper.limitations: The evidence concerns tDCS only, with heterogeneous protocols and outcomes, low quality, and uncertain durability, safety, and real-world relevance.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not add brain stimulation to routine performance practice. Any exploratory use requires appropriate medical, ethical, regulatory, and safety governance.
paper.athleteDev: Set clear expectations that neurotechnology marketing exceeds the certainty of current sport-performance evidence.
paper.rtp: Non-invasive brain stimulation is not a rehabilitation or return-to-sport intervention on this evidence.

records.sourceFile: Sleep interventions for performance, mood and sleep outcomes in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Gwyther K, Rice SM, Purcell R, Pilkington V, Santesteban-Echarri O, Bailey A, Walton CC. Sleep Interventions for Performance, Mood and Sleep Outcomes in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Psychology of Sport and Exercise. 2022;58:102094.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis assessed sleep interventions for athlete sleep, mood, and performance outcomes.
paper.tldr: Sleep interventions improved subjective sleep quality, sleepiness, and negative affect, but did not show objective sleep or aerobic and anaerobic performance benefit in the controlled evidence.
paper.methods: Five databases returned 5,996 records; 27 studies involving 617 athletes were included, and 12 controlled trials entered random-effects meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Interventions improved subjective sleep quality (g=0.62), reduced sleepiness (g=0.81), and reduced negative affect (g=0.63), with no identified effect on objective sleep measures or aerobic and anaerobic performance indices.
paper.limitations: Studies were small and non-representative, with varied interventions and outcomes and methodological concerns. Objective performance evidence was limited.
paper.practicalImplications: Start with individualized behavioral and environmental sleep support, identify the desired outcome, and monitor response rather than promising performance gains.
paper.athleteDev: Separate sleep-support habits from performance guarantees and encourage early discussion of persistent sleep problems or medication use.
paper.rtp: Sleep support can assist overall recovery planning but does not substitute for clinical, tissue, and sport-exposure criteria during return to sport.
